cards.text: Lamentations is a book of tears over Jerusalem after her people fell into the hands of the enemy (Lamentations 1:7). The writer just asked why any mortal man should complain, in view of his sins (Lamentations 3:39). Now he speaks for all his people.

cards.question: After asking why anyone should complain in view of his sins, what does the writer call everyone to do?

answers.text: Test how they live and turn back to God
Rebuild the walls and wait for rescue
Leave the city and start over elsewhere

cards.text: Then the writer calls everyone to lift up their hearts and hands to God in heaven. Hearts AND hands, friend, because waving your hands with your heart left at home is just stretching.

cards.question: In the prayer the people lift up to God, they confess that they have ___ and rebelled.
In that same prayer, the people tell God He has already forgiven them.

cards.text: No forgiveness. The words keep going, straight to God, and they get heavy: “You have covered Yourself in anger and pursued us; You have killed without pity.”

cards.question: The writer says God has covered Himself with a cloud. What can't pass through that cloud?
Among the nations, what does the writer say God has made him and his people?
The writer says all the foes of his people keep their mouths shut and stay silent.

cards.text: Panic and pitfall have come upon them, devastation and destruction. The writer stacks the words two at a time, and I bet he feels overwhelmed.
Then it gets personal, and the writer speaks for himself. He says, “Streams of tears flow from my eyes over the destruction of the daughter of my people.”

cards.question: The writer's eyes overflow without relief. How long does he say they'll keep overflowing?

answers.text: Until the LORD looks down and sees
Until the foes leave the land
Until the city walls go back up

cards.question: The writer's eyes bring grief to his soul because of all the daughters of his city.

cards.text: Now the writer tells what his enemies did to him. Without cause, they hunted him like a bird.

cards.question: The enemies who hunted the writer caught him. Where did they drop him?

cards.text: Then they cast stones on him, and the waters flowed over his head. This part is heavy, friend.

cards.question: With the waters flowing over his head, the writer thought he was going to ___.
Out of the depths of the Pit, what does the writer do?

answers.text: He calls on the LORD's name
He goes quiet and gives up

cards.text: Friend, I spent years in the back of a junk drawer, and NOBODY heard a peep out of me. But this man calls from the Pit, and the LORD hears his plea: “Do not ignore my cry for relief.”

cards.question: When the writer called on the LORD from the Pit, what did the LORD say to him?
After the LORD drew near, the writer says the Lord defends his cause and redeems his life.

cards.text: Then the writer lays it out plain: the LORD has seen the wrong done to him.

cards.question: Right after saying the LORD has seen the wrong done to him, the writer asks the LORD to vindicate his cause.

cards.text: The LORD has seen all the malice and plots against the writer, and heard the insults, slander and murmuring of his attackers all day long. ALL DAY LONG, friend, like a group chat about you that never goes quiet.

cards.question: The writer's enemies keep at it when they sit and when they rise. How does he say they mock him?
The writer says the LORD will let his enemies go free.

cards.text: The writer says the LORD will pay his enemies back what they deserve, according to the work of their hands. Then he asks the LORD to put a veil of anguish over their hearts: “may Your curse be upon them!”

cards.question: Back at the start, the writer said God had pursued his people in anger. At the very end, he says the LORD will pursue his people in anger again.

cards.text: The writer's last words turn it around: the LORD will pursue his enemies in anger and exterminate them from under His heavens.
